data.anchortopology-follow-an-edge-or-corner#:
AnchorTopology is a named component datum that stays attached to native SolidCraft topology. edge picks an edge, on selects its adjacent planar face and corner optionally chooses one endpoint. The coordinates are selection picks; SolidCraft keeps the selected edge, face and endpoint by topology name as the design changes.
from scpf import AnchorTopology, Box, component @component class Board: def anchors(self): return { "mount": AnchorTopology( edge=(-20, 50, 5), on=(-20, 50, 10), corner=(-20, 0, 5), z=(0, 1, 0), x=(0, 0, 1), ) } def build(self): return Box(40, 100, 20) This is useful for references such as the straight tangent edge beside a fillet: if dimensions move that edge, the joint can follow it without freezing the original XYZ point. The current implementation supports named or direct AnchorTopology values on non-rotated occurrences. A direct topology anchor is useful when the datum belongs only to one assembly rather than to the reusable component. SCPF deliberately does not transform topology picks itself.
SolidCraft joints remain an internal implementation detail; Forge does not expose a separate public Joint object.
data.assembly-owned-named-anchors#Assembly-ow:
When a datum belongs to the meaning of an assembly rather than to a generic component, keep it on the assembly with with_anchor(). The anchor stores the target occurrence plus its attachment reference. Consumers resolve it by name with anchor().
frame = (left + right + bottom).with_anchor( "front_top_left", left, AnchorTopology( edge=(-6, 0, 181), on=(0, 0, 181), corner=(-6, 0, 362), z=(0, 0, -1), x=(1, 0, 0), ), ) parent = frame.anchor("front_top_left") bracket = CornerBracket().attach( parent.target, parent=parent.reference, child=bracket_reference, ) This keeps a generic Board or CornerBracket free of application-specific anchor names while a higher-level frame can expose semantic datums such as front_top_left.
An assembly anchor may also carry its own symbolic offset=(u, v). Consumers can combine that semantic offset with a fixed local correction and pass the result to attach(offset=...). This is useful when an assembly datum follows a frame parameter such as wall thickness while the reusable part keeps a fixed mounting correction.
data.associative-in-plane-attachment-offset#A:
attach(offset=(u, v)) moves the child within the attachment plane. Numeric values and parameter expressions are both supported. Forge lowers a non-zero or symbolic in-plane offset to a native planar joint and keeps u and v as SolidCraft joint values, so they are re-evaluated when their parameters change.
wood = Parameter("wood_thickness", 18) bracket = Bracket().attach( side, parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT, child=mount, offset=(0, -wood + 12), gap=-12, ) offset is independent of gap: the two offset values move in the attachment plane, while gap remains the normal distance between the two references. On a rectangular corner origin, the second planar value follows the selected vertical corner edge; its sign is defined by that corner frame rather than by world Z.
data.component-attachment#Component attachmen: right = BeamComponent().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT ) marker = Marker().attach( frame, parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_RIGHT, child=Anchor.BACK_TOP_RIGHT, ) attach() is the public Forge relationship between reusable components. Anchor selects the attachment reference: a supported face, or one of the eight rectangular corners such as FRONT_TOP_RIGHT. Corner anchors compile to native SolidCraft edge/corner origins, so they follow dimension changes in a saved design.
data.component-parameter-visibility#Component:
Reusable component defaults are fixed by default. Publish selected child parameters explicitly with include=:
@component(include=("inside_corner_radius",)) class CornerBracket: width = 24.0 inside_corner_radius = 4.0 def build(self): ... When a parent Parameter or expression is passed into a child input, that existing dependency stays symbolic. For example, CornerBracket(inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius) reuses the parent design’s corner_radius; it does not create a separate CornerBracket_inside_corner_radius parameter.
data.occurrence-placement#Occurrence placemen:
copy() retains the source Placement when no override is supplied. copy(placement=Placement(...)) creates the new occurrence with the supplied absolute pose in the parent coordinate frame. The compiler uses creation-time copy translation where SolidCraft can represent it and a native fallback only where required.
center = BeamComponent() array = center for x in (-240, -120, 120, 240): array = array + center.copy(placement=Placement(x=x))
data.one-definition-several-occurrences#One d:
from scpf import Box, assembly, component @component class Beam: length = 100.0 def build(self): return Box(self.length, 20, 20) @assembly class BeamPair: spacing = 120.0 def build(self): left = Beam() right = left.copy(placement=Placement(x=self.spacing)) return (left + right).group("Beams") pair = BeamPair() @component marks one reusable physical part. Its build() returns the complete geometry/feature tree for that part; that tree may be made from many primitives and features. @assembly marks a class whose build() composes separate component occurrences. Both decorators return callable model objects, so normal model code stays readable as Beam() and BeamPair().
SolidCraft receives one reusable definition and multiple occurrences. A group is a native parent component in the browser, not a Boolean fusion of its children.
data.what-to-test-in-an-assembly#What to test: Check the native command list for one component.create per shared definition, expected occurrence.copy counts, and native translate, axis and angle parameters for rotated occurrences. Separately verify native SolidCraft geometry and its bounding dimensions before trusting an assembly image.

data.a-feature-changes-an-existing-body#A fea: A native feature is different from subtracting arbitrary CSG geometry. SCPF can retain named sketches and operations in SolidCraft history. For exact results, supported body types and selection constraints matter.
data.feature-placement-without-hard-coded-glo: from scpf import X, Y, Boss, Anchor boss = Boss(d=7, h=12, hole_d=2.5).attach( case, parent=Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM, offset=(X.MIN + 10, Y.MAX - 10), ) X.MIN and Y.MAX refer to the parent bounds and are not rotation-axis constants. Anchoring support currently focuses on rectangular bases and a documented set of faces. Do not assume every curved or lofted surface supports it.
data.fillets-and-chamfers#Fillets and chamfer: from scpf import FRONT, LEFT, Box, Edges body = Box(80, 50, 15) rounded = body.fillet(3, edges=Edges.VERTICAL) bevelled = body.chamfer(3, edges=Edges.VERTICAL) one_edge = body.chamfer(3, edges=FRONT + LEFT) fillet() and chamfer() use the same edge-selection forms. Use Edges.VERTICAL for all vertical edges of a supported rectangular body, a two-direction selector such as FRONT + LEFT for one Box edge, Edges.from_profile(...) or Edges.from_vertices(...) for named Polygon2D geometry, or explicit XYZ pick coordinates. Both methods default to Edges.VERTICAL. A topological edge cannot always be inferred reliably from a visual camera position.
data.holes#Holes: from scpf import Box, Hole, Depth, Faces plate = Box(100, 60, 10) hole = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL) plate = plate + hole.on(plate, face=Faces.TOP) A Hole is a native hole feature: adding it to the shape means adding the operation that removes material. Faces.TOP selects its entry face. Simple feature placement uses on(); assembly attachment uses explicit anchors.
data.native-feature-patterns#Native feature p:
Pattern an already-applied native feature when the copies should remain one editable SolidCraft history operation. Rectangular and circular patterns share the same source-feature rules: pass the same Forge Shape object that was applied to the body. Forge resolves that object to its native history feature; callers never manage SolidCraft timeline-name strings. Direct native Hole-family and primitive features are supported alongside the existing Sketch.extrude() path, and a direct count Parameter remains editable in the saved design.
from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Hole plate = Box(100, 80, 6, anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM) bolt_hole = Hole( d=8, direction=(0, 0, -1), ).at(30, 0, 6) plate = plate + bolt_hole bolt_circle = plate.circular_pattern( bolt_hole, count=6, axis=Axis.Z, ) circular_pattern() omits angle by default so SolidCraft uses its native 360-degree full-circle behaviour. Supply a fixed degree value or direct Parameter for a partial arc. origin=(x, y, z) moves a fixed axis; a fixed non-zero XYZ vector can be used instead of Axis.X/Y/Z. Construction-axis and geometry-axis selectors are not yet exposed by Forge.
grid = plate.rectangular_pattern( bolt_hole, count=4, spacing=20, direction=Axis.X, count2=3, spacing2=18, direction2=Axis.Y, ) rectangular_pattern() and circular_pattern() both emit one native feature-pattern command rather than expanding independent copies in Python.
data.shells#Shells: from scpf import Box, Faces case = Box(80, 50, 30).shell(2, open=Faces.TOP) Faces.TOP chooses the face to open and is also the same surface-selection vocabulary used by feature.on(...). Anchor is reserved for explicit component attachment in assemblies. See the source and regression tests for supported feature chains.

data.add-subtract-and-intersect#Add, subtract: body = Box(50, 50, 20) tool = Cylinder(d=12, h=22).at(0, 0, 0) joined = body + tool # union, where supported cut = body - tool # difference, where supported shared = body & tool # intersection, where supported The supported compiler path depends on the operands. Native feature history and CSG trees are not interchangeable for every operation. For manufacturing features such as holes, prefer the native feature operations.
data.draw-a-2d-profile-then-extrude-it#Draw a:
A Rectangle2D is a planar profile rather than a 3D body. 2D geometry is authored inside an explicit Sketch scope. Polygon2D can be created on the XY, XZ or YZ plane.
from scpf import Sketch, Rectangle2D, Polygon2D with Sketch(plane="XY") as plate_sketch: Rectangle2D(80, 50) plate = plate_sketch.extrude(8) with Sketch(plane="XZ") as side_sketch: Polygon2D( [(0, 0), (40, 0), (40, 8), (8, 8), (8, 30), (0, 30)], plane="XZ", world=True, ) side = side_sketch.extrude(10) # Signed distance chooses the side of the sketch plane. backward = plate_sketch.extrude(-8) centered = plate_sketch.extrude(8, sym=True) A sketch plane affects where its axes go; changing the camera does not rotate its geometry. Leave the with Sketch(...) scope, then call sketch.extrude(...) to create 3D material. A positive distance follows the sketch-plane normal, a negative distance goes the other way, and sym=True divides a positive distance equally over both sides. Direct Rectangle2D(...).extrude(...) syntax is intentionally not supported.
Polygon2D works in standalone explicit Sketches and in face-attached explicit Sketches; its authored vertices stay sketch-local. Standalone Sketches may also use an explicit origin= and rotation=(rx, ry, rz). An extrusion from that rotated local frame can participate directly in +, - or & CSG, including non-axis-aligned cutters.
data.repeat-and-mirror-profiles-inside-one-sk:
Sketch.rectangular_pattern() makes a native SolidCraft sketch pattern from a profile that already belongs to the Sketch. Sketch.mirror() mirrors a profile, a pattern result or an earlier mirror result. Both methods return a Sketch result that can be passed to another supported Sketch operation.
from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Circle2D, Depth, Sketch board = Box(200, 120, 8) with Sketch(name="Dog holes", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as holes: seed = holes.add(Circle2D(d=8), offset=(-40, 20)) row = holes.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=4, spacing=25, direction=Axis.X, ) holes.mirror(row, axis=Axis.X) board = board - holes.extrude(Depth.THROUGH_ALL) The same operations work with native Slot profiles. A pattern or mirror result can be used as the source of the next operation.
from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Sketch, SlotCenterToCenter2D with Sketch(name="Clamp slots", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as slots: seed = SlotCenterToCenter2D((20, 20), (40, 20), 8) arm = slots.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=2, spacing=50, direction=Axis.X, ) opposite = slots.mirror(arm, axis=Axis.Y) slots.mirror(arm, axis=Axis.X) slots.mirror(opposite, axis=Axis.X) count, count2, spacing and spacing2 may use suitable model Parameters, so those values remain editable in the saved SolidCraft design. Current native qualification covers attached Sketch(on=...) use. Pattern directions support Axis.X, Axis.Y or a fixed 2D vector. Mirrors currently support the Sketch X or Y origin axis. Per-instance pattern suppression is not supported.
SolidCraft 0.42 stores the curves selected when a mirror is created. If a pattern later creates extra curves after its count changes, those new curves are not added to that existing mirror automatically.
data.select-profiles-when-extruding-a-sketch#:
By default Sketch.extrude() uses every closed profile in the Sketch. Use profiles=[(x, y), ...] when only some closed regions should be extruded or cut. The points are fixed coordinates in the Sketch itself; users do not need SolidCraft profile indices or curve ids.
from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Circle2D, Depth, Sketch board = Box(120, 80, 5, anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM) with Sketch(name="Selected holes", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as holes: seed = holes.add(Circle2D(d=8), offset=(-30, 0)) holes.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=4, spacing=20, direction=Axis.X, ) board = board - holes.extrude( Depth.THROUGH_ALL, profiles=[(-30, 0), (-10, 0), (30, 0)], exact_regions=True, ) SolidCraft 0.42 stores a successful point selection using the curves around the selected profile where possible. That lets the selection follow the profile when the saved design recomputes. exact_regions=True asks SolidCraft to use exactly the region containing each point. Profile points must be fixed finite numbers; Forge Parameters and expressions are not accepted in this field.
data.start-with-a-solid#Start with a solid:
Box, Cylinder and Sphere are centred on their geometric CENTER by default. Use anchor=... when a face, axial end or tangent datum should lie at the origin. For Cylinder the anchor is resolved after choosing Axis.X, Axis.Y or Axis.Z; for example LEFT/RIGHT are the axial ends of an X-axis cylinder and BOTTOM/TOP are the axial ends of a Z-axis cylinder.
from scpf import ( BOTTOM, FRONT, LEFT, RIGHT, Axis, Box, Cylinder, Sphere, ) plate = Box(80, 50, 8) board = Box(80, 50, 12).at( 0, 0, 0, anchor=FRONT + BOTTOM, ).fillet( 4, edges=[BOTTOM + LEFT, BOTTOM + RIGHT], ) pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.Z).at( 10, 10, 8, anchor=BOTTOM, ) side_pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at(-10, 0, 0) ball = Sphere(12) body = Sphere(20) & Box(30, 30, 30) centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body) at(x, y, z) places CENTER at those coordinates unless another anchor=... is supplied. Passing another Shape instead uses shape-relative CENTER-to-CENTER placement. Forge derives the native Box corner, Cylinder base or Sphere center from the selected datum; callers do not add manual half-size corrections.

data.compile-inspect-then-execute#Compile, in:
Save the model as model.py. Compilation alone does not open SolidCraft. The JSON is a native command plan, not a mesh or STEP file.
python -m scpf model.py --out output/model.json python -m json.tool output/model.json For a live GUI run, open SolidCraft, enable Preferences → Assistant → Let AI agents connect, and use:
python -m scpf model.py --connect --new --new asks SolidCraft to replace the active design with a new, empty one before the model batch is sent. Leave it off when you deliberately want to add commands to the current design. Neither form saves the design. The CAD project also provides a separate native CLI qualification workflow.
data.install-the-library#Install the library:
In the lib.py.solidcraft.forge repository and an active Python environment:
python -m pip install -e ./scpf python -m unittest discover -s scpf/tests -v
data.what-scpf-does#What SCPF does: SCPF is a Python interface and compiler for native SolidCraft commands. It is not a replacement CAD kernel. You describe a model using ordinary Python; SolidCraft executes the generated commands and owns the final geometry and feature history.
data.where-to-continue#Where to continue: Read Model objects first. Then read Positioning and orientation. That chapter explains the practical difference between at(), on(), Shape.attach(), Placement and Occurrence.attach(). After that, From one component to an assembly shows how separate physical parts are combined.
data.your-first-model#Your first model:
Define one class, give it numeric dimensions, and return the body from build(). No main() or show() is necessary.
from scpf import Box, Edges class Plate: length = 100.0 width = 60.0 thickness = 10.0 def build(self): plate = Box(self.length, self.width, self.thickness) return plate.fillet(2, edges=Edges.VERTICAL) Plate()

data.a-model-is-a-normal-python-class#A model:
Numeric class attributes become editable SolidCraft parameters when SCPF compiles a plain model class. build() returns geometry. If a file contains exactly one public class with build(), that class is the root automatically; no trailing constructor call or launcher file is needed.
from scpf import Box class Plate: length = 100.0 width = 60.0 thickness = 10.0 def build(self): return Box(self.length, self.width, self.thickness) Run that source file directly with python -m scpf plate.py --connect. The same rule lets a reusable component file serve as its standalone model while assemblies import the exact same class. If a file contains several public model classes, SCPF deliberately does not guess: finish the script with an explicit call such as Assembly() to choose the root.
An explicit final call is also how you override root parameters for a particular run, for example Plate(width=80). Arithmetic such as self.length / 2 is preserved symbolically for supported expressions; general Python computations are not automatically made parametric.
data.groups-are-actual-native-parent-componen: blocks = (first + second).group("Blocks") Grouping changes the browser hierarchy, not the geometry’s orientation. At present one shared definition cannot be split among different groups.
data.important-boundaries#Important boundarie:
Associative attachment is supported for a limited set of rectangular component faces. General mates, arbitrary face queries and rotational constraints are not implemented as a complete assembly solver.
Next:Positioning and orientation explains how to place geometry and component occurrences, and when at(), on() or attach() is the right choice.
data.parameter-intent-is-visible-in-the-name#:
SCPF distinguishes three kinds of numeric class attributes. This keeps a Python build setting from looking like a native editable CAD parameter.
class Display: PANEL_COUNT = 5 # fixed constant _panel_pitch = 160.0 # Forge/build-time input opening_width = 844.0 # native model parameter Name Meaning SolidCraft parameter UPPER_CASE Fixed constant No _lower_case Forge/build-time input No lower_case Editable model parameter Yes If a public lower-case parameter is consumed only as a concrete Python value—for example through pv()—Forge emits a ModelParameterWarning. The same warning is emitted when a parameter remains native in some geometry but is also flattened into concrete occurrence placement. Such a parameter is only partly associative: editing it in SolidCraft would update only part of the model. Keep Placement coordinates symbolic or rename an intentionally build-time input with a leading underscore.
data.shape-versus-component-occurrence#Shape:
Shape describes geometry or a feature expression (Box, Hole, an extrusion). A component occurrence is one placed instance of a shared, editable model definition. Do not confuse a new occurrence with a new feature history.
from scpf import Box, Placement, component class Block: def build(self): return Box(40, 20, 10) BlockComponent = component(Block) first = BlockComponent(placement=Placement(x=-25)) second = first.copy(placement=Placement(x=25)) assembly = first + second The two occurrences share the same Block definition. Placement is occurrence creation metadata: XYZ is absolute in the parent coordinate frame and optional rotation adds orientation. The component definition never receives placement as a model parameter.
data.share-one-model-parameter-across-child-c:
Passing a parent parameter into several component inputs keeps one native SolidCraft parameter instead of creating component-specific duplicates.
bottom = BottomBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius) roof = RoofBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius) bracket = Bracket( bracket_width=self.bracket_width, inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius, ) Here the wooden fillets and bracket inside fillet all depend on the same corner_radius. Passing the parent parameter into the child input reuses that existing native dependency rather than creating a duplicate child parameter.
Reusable component defaults stay fixed unless they are explicitly published with include=. Parent Parameters/Expressions passed into child inputs always stay symbolic and reuse the existing parent dependency.
Bracket = component( CornerBracket, include=("inside_corner_radius",), ) # Or publish all public defaults explicitly: FullyEditableBracket = component(CornerBracket, include="*") This publication rule is recorded in change 0003.

data.apply-a-whole-sheet-perforation-field#Ap:
sheet = sheet.perforate( diameter=5, pitch=10, margin=5, pattern="square", ) Shape.perforate() adds native manufacturing perforation semantics to existing sheet material. Diameter and pitch are positive millimetre dimensions. margin is optional; omitting it leaves SolidCraft’s native diameter-sized margin default in control. pattern is staggered by default or may be square.
The first Forge contract applies to the whole sheet. It deliberately does not expose SolidCraft’s Sketch/profile-bounded region fields. Perforations remain flat-pattern/DXF/measurement semantics rather than repeated B-rep holes.
data.create-a-flat-sheet-body#Create a flat s: with Sketch(name="Blank", plane="XY") as sketch: Rectangle2D(80, 40) sheet = sketch.sheet_metal( thickness=2, bend_radius=2, k_factor=0.5, rule_name="Panel sheet", ) Sketch.sheet_metal() creates a new sheet body from one closed Sketch. It is a body-creation operation, not a feature applied to an existing sheet.
data.create-a-sheet-from-an-open-contour#Crea: with Sketch(name="Contour", plane="XZ") as sketch: chain = sketch.chain(start=(0, 0)) chain.line_to((35, 0)) chain.tangent_arc_to((40, 5)) chain.line_to((40, 30)) contour = chain.finish() sheet = contour.contour_flange( distance=50, thickness=2.5, bend_radius=2.5, k_factor=0.44, ) Shape.contour_flange() is the other body-creation operation. Its receiver is a finished connected open Sketch chain. Forge preserves chain order and replay-bound native curve identity; callers do not pass SolidCraft curve ids.
data.editable-dimensions-versus-topology-pick: Keep design dimensions symbolic when the method accepts Parameter/Expression values. Current edge picks and straight fold-line coordinates are intentionally fixed finite coordinates. Forge rejects unsupported associative selectors instead of pretending a numeric pick is a stable topology reference.
data.fold-existing-material#Fold existing mat: sheet = sheet.fold( line=((20, -20, 0), (20, 20, 0)), angle=90, fixed=(-30, 0, 0), ) Shape.fold() bends material that already belongs to the sheet. The initial contract uses one straight fixed-coordinate fold line. Thickness, K-factor and bend radius come from the active rule.
data.follow-a-reusable-path#Follow a reusable: with Sketch(name="Path", plane="XZ") as sketch: chain = sketch.chain(start=(0, 0)) chain.line_to((0, 14)) path = chain.finish() sheet = sheet.path_flange( edge=(40, 0, 2), path=path, radius=3, ) Shape.path_flange() adds a native flange to an existing edge using a finished open Sketch path. The qualified SolidCraft 0.45 contract is line-only. Omitting radius inherits the active rule; supplying it overrides only this feature’s bend radius.
data.grow-an-edge-flange#Grow an edge flange: sheet = sheet.flange( edges=[(40, 0, 2)], height=20, angle=90, ) Shape.flange() adds material to explicit existing sheet edges. Height and angle may remain parameterized. Edge selection is currently a non-empty set of fixed XYZ pick points; generic topology selectors are not yet part of this API.
data.hem-an-existing-edge#Hem an existing edg: sheet = sheet.hem( edges=[(40, 0, 2)], length=12, gap=4, ) Shape.hem() folds an existing edge back onto the sheet while inheriting the active material rule. The first contract uses fixed XYZ edge picks. Length and optional gap are feature dimensions and may be parameterized.
data.one-sheet-rule-owns-the-material#One she: A sheet body has one active rule. That rule owns thickness, k_factor and the default bend_radius. Operations on an existing sheet inherit those values instead of restating them. Feature-specific dimensions such as flange height, hem length or a path-flange radius override remain on the feature.
data.sheet-metal-is-native-editable-history#S: Forge sheet-metal operations lower to SolidCraft sheet rules and native sheet features. Use them when the saved design must keep material thickness, bend allowance and a recoverable flat pattern. Do not replace these operations with fused solid envelopes when native history matters.
data.verification-and-flat-patterns#Verificat: Native sheet-metal verification is stronger than matching a formed bounding box. Verification cases inspect sheet-rule values, native bend/history records, saved-design parameter edits and the recoverable flat pattern. See the Verification catalog, especially the Sheet metal group.

data.copies-can-have-different-placements#Cop: first = Panel( placement=Placement(z=160, rotation=(X, 90)) ) second = first.copy( placement=Placement(x=160, z=160, rotation=(X, 90)) ) screen = first + second The two occurrences reuse one component definition but have different placements. copy() without a placement override keeps the source Placement.
data.current-limits#Current limits: Operation Current meaning Shape.at(...) Absolute geometry placement; shape-to-shape alignment is currently CENTER-to-CENTER. Shape.on(...) Supported within-part feature placement on TOP or BOTTOM. Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Placement(...) Absolute occurrence pose with one optional axis-angle rotation. Occurrence.attach(...) Assembly relationship between separate component occurrences.
data.shapeattach-is-lower-level-within-part-p:
from scpf import Anchor, Boss, X, Y boss = Boss(d=7, h=12, hole_d=2.5).attach( case, parent=Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM, offset=(X.MIN + 10, Y.MAX - 10), ) Use Shape.attach() only when a simple on() face does not express the required feature reference. It lets you choose explicit parent and child anchors.
This does not create an assembly joint. The feature and target are still geometry inside one part.
data.shapemove-is-a-local-geometry-translatio: body = Box(40, 20, 10) shifted = body.move(x=10, y=0, z=25) move() translates supported geometry inside its current shape expression. It is not the normal way to position a component occurrence. Use Placement for occurrences.
data.start-with-the-coordinate-system#Start w:
X, Y and Z are model axes. A normal Box has its large base in XY and thickness along Z. A camera rotation changes only the view. It does not change the model coordinates.
Also separate two levels: geometry inside one part has its own coordinates; a component occurrence has a pose in the assembly.
data.use-at-to-place-or-align-geometry#Use at:
from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Cylinder pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at( 10, 0, 5, anchor=Anchor.LEFT, ) body = Box(80, 50, 12) centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body) shape.at(x, y, z) places supported geometry at an absolute model coordinate. A primitive can use anchor=... to say which of its own datums belongs at that coordinate.
shape.at(target) currently aligns CENTER to CENTER. It does not mean “put this on the top face”. For a feature on a face, use on().
data.use-occurrenceattach-for-separate-physic:
from scpf import Anchor left = Block() right = Block().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, ) assembly = left + right Here right is a separate physical part. Its rule is not an absolute XYZ position; its left side belongs on the right side of left. That is an assembly relationship, so use Occurrence.attach().
SolidCraft stores this as a native joint. If the parent changes size, the relationship can still express which references belong together. The next chapter, From one component to an assembly, builds on this distinction.
data.use-on-for-a-feature-on-a-face#Use on():
from scpf import Box, Depth, Faces, Hole plate = Box(100, 60, 10) hole = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL).on( plate, face=Faces.TOP, offset=(20, 0), ) plate = plate + hole on() is for a feature that belongs to an existing shape. Faces.TOP or Faces.BOTTOM selects the face where the feature starts or is supported. The offset is measured in that face.
A sketch has the same idea in explicit form: Sketch(on=body, parent=Anchor.TOP) creates a named sketch on a selected body face.
data.use-placement-for-a-component-occurrence:
from scpf import Placement, X, Z, component @component class Panel: def build(self): return Box(160, 320, 14.5) first = Panel() second = first.copy( placement=Placement(x=160, z=20) ) upright = first.copy( placement=Placement( z=160, rotation=(X, 90), ) ) upside_down = first.copy( placement=Placement(rotation=(Z, 180)) ) Placement describes the complete pose of one component occurrence in its parent coordinate frame. XYZ is absolute. The optional rotation is one axis-angle orientation.
Placement does not say that one component depends on another. It only says where this occurrence is.
data.which-one-do-i-use#Which one do I use?:
These APIs all affect where something ends up, but they mean different things. Choose the one that matches the rule in the model.
You want to… Use What it means Place or align geometry inside one part shape.at(...) Geometric placement. No joint or assembly relationship is created. Put a feature on a face of another shape feature.on(...) Within-part feature placement. The selected Faces value chooses the support or entry face. Place a feature with explicit parent/child anchors Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Prefer on() when a simple face is enough. Give one component occurrence an absolute pose Placement(...) Position and optional orientation at occurrence creation/copy time. No joint is created. Relate two separate physical component occurrences Occurrence.attach(...) An assembly relationship that SolidCraft stores as a native joint. The important distinction:Shape.attach() and Occurrence.attach() have the same verb but work at different levels. The first places a feature inside one part. The second relates two separate component occurrences.

data.keep-implementation-and-docs-in-sync#Kee:
When placement syntax changes, add tests for the exact generated native commands before documenting it as supported. Named principal-axis rotation is supported; chained rotations are still not.
For a plain-language explanation of the implementation and its boundaries, read How SCPF works (without building a second CAD engine).
data.native-geometric-verification#Native geo: The CAD model repository runs a separate SolidCraft CLI workflow for native geometry, editable history, STEP output, measurements and screenshots. Read the saved SolidCraft occurrence transforms, not just whether a command ran successfully. A valid Python object or syntactically valid command plan is not evidence that the final solid occupies the correct plane or has no collision.
data.test-compiled-native-commands#Test compi: Compare the generated command structure with explicit expectations, not only with a count of operations. Tests should check component names, requested positions, the orientation axis and angle, and feature ordering. A regression can preserve a known good JSON fixture when command ordering is part of the contract.
data.unit-tests-for-python-behavior#Unit test:
The library’s tests under scpf/tests/ cover model objects, feature compilation, reusable components and rotation validation. For example, an occurrence rotation test checks that the compiler emits one occurrence.move with the expected native parameters.
python -m unittest discover -s scpf/tests -v

data.1-start-with-the-real-construction#1. St:
The verification use case is an open wooden frame. A neutral CornerBracket connects a side board to the top or bottom board.
4 brackets One bracket at each side-to-top/bottom connection on the front edge. 8 brackets Repeat exactly the same four connections at the rear edge. Later: 3D corner One true corner component on all eight corners of a box.
Front and rear are positions, not boards. There is no front or rear board in this relationship. They only identify which end of the cabinet depth receives the bracket.
data.3-where-does-the-joint-origin-frame-come: Left: frame topology. Right: explicit child joint origin on the bracket. CadCraft source · DXF
data.4-zoom-in-what-do-x-and-z-mean-at-the-fo:
The current HUB75 model gives us a concrete example. The bracket geometry has its own model axes. The joint origin then defines another local frame on that geometry.
The bracket’s model axes and the current assembly-local joint frames. CadCraft source · DXF
Do not mix these two coordinate systems.+X/+Y/+Z describe the bracket model. Lower-case joint x and z describe the frame SolidCraft uses to mate that bracket. For example, joint x = -Z means that the joint-frame x-axis points in the bracket model’s negative-Z direction.
data.5-what-the-current-forge-code-is-doing#5:
The current fixture first defines the child joint origin in Python:
bracket_corner = AnchorFrame( origin=(0, 0, 0), z=Anchor.FRONT, x=Anchor.RIGHT, ) and then uses it in the assembly:
bracket.copy().attach( frame, parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT, child=bracket_corner, angle=0, ) The low-level vectors are still the real data, but ordinary model code no longer has to spell the six principal directions numerically. The readable constants make the intent visible while keeping the mapping to SolidCraft direct.
data.6-requirements-for-the-forge-api#6. Requ: The generated data must map directly to SolidCraft’s own joint-origin information. No second orientation solver in Python. CornerBracket must remain independent of the cabinet: no left/right, top/bottom, front/rear or cabinet dimensions. Forge must not guess orientation from a class name or from bracket geometry. Normal model code should not require raw vectors such as z=(0,-1,0) and x=(1,0,0). The low-level vector representation may remain available for genuinely low-level use. The solution is qualified first with four brackets, then eight, then a true 3D corner component. Chosen API: keep AnchorFrame(origin, z, x), use the cardinal Anchor members as readable direction vectors, and keep arbitrary vectors available for non-axis-aligned frames. Forge does not guess any additional orientation.
data.7-verification-order#7. Verification ord: Case What it proves 4 brackets The same neutral bracket works at all four front side-to-top/bottom connections. 8 brackets The same bracket and same child joint-origin definition also work at the rear edge. Resize Width, height and depth changes are re-solved from native references without rerunning Python. 3D corner Only after the above: one true corner component on all eight box corners.
data.child-b-explicit-point-frame#Child B: ex:
The current fixture chooses a point on the bracket and supplies z and x. If a point origin omits x, SolidCraft chooses x from z alone, so a part that was deliberately spun around z can turn back when joined.
Calling B a “local reference” is too vague. On this page we use the precise term child joint origin.
data.conceptual-api-object#Conceptual API obj:
In a generic API the same local frame can be described explicitly with a point and two directions:
{ "joint_origin": { "name": "beugel_bevestigingspunt_1", "description": "Midden van het bovenste schroefgat", "origin": { "x": 10.0, "y": 25.0, "z": 0.0 }, "axes": { "z_direction": [0, 0, 1], "x_direction": [1, 0, 0], "y_direction": "auto_calculated" } } } origin is the position. z_direction tells which way the local frame faces. x_direction fixes the remaining clocking around Z. Y does not need to be authored separately.
data.depth-view-four-becomes-eight#Depth view:
The first verification uses the front row only; the eight-bracket case repeats the same four connections at the rear. CadCraft source · DXF
The bracket itself knows only its own local geometry. It does not know left/right, top/bottom, front/rear or the dimensions of the cabinet. The assembly chooses those placements.
data.english--simple-explanation#English — si:
A joint origin on a bracket is the digital attachment point used to connect the part. The easiest way to understand it is as a small local coordinate system with its own X, Y and Z axes.
Origin: the exact point where the local coordinate system starts, for example the centre of a screw hole. Z axis (normal): defines which way the attachment point faces. X axis (clocking): once Z is fixed, X fixes the remaining rotation around Z. Y axis (automatic): once Z and X are known, the third perpendicular axis follows automatically. origin = where is the point? Z = which way does it face? X = how is it rotated around that direction? Y = calculated automatically SolidCraft mates joint origin B to joint origin A. CadCraft source · DXF
data.four-front-corners-one-by-one#Four front:
Four enlarged front-corner placements. The parent topology frame rotates around the frame; the current child definition is reused. CadCraft source · DXF
Corner Parent anchor Child point Parent z Parent x Current child input Top left Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT A -Y -Z z=+Y, x=-Z Top right Anchor.FRONT_TOP_RIGHT B -Y -X z=+Y, x=-Z Bottom right Anchor.FRONT_BOTTOM_RIGHT A -Y +Z z=+Y, x=-Z Bottom left Anchor.FRONT_BOTTOM_LEFT B -Y +X z=+Y, x=-Z Notice what changes: the parent x-axis rotates with the selected corner. The raw child-frame definition for the front row does not change. When SolidCraft solves the joint, the bracket occurrence rotates so its child frame mates with that parent frame.
data.front-view-the-brackets-are-outside-the-: Four outside brackets. The opening stays free and no bracket is drawn inside the wood. CadCraft source · DXF
data.native-solidcraft-references#Native Soli: Command reference — joint.origin / joint.create Components and joints guide
data.nederlands--eenvoudige-uitleg#Nederlands:
Een joint origin op een bracket (beugel) is het digitale ankerpunt waarmee je het onderdeel vastzet. Je kunt dit het beste zien als een klein lokaal assenstelsel met een eigen X-, Y- en Z-as.
Origin (het nulpunt): het precieze punt op de beugel waar het lokale assenstelsel begint, bijvoorbeeld het midden van een schroefgat. Z-as (de normaal): bepaalt welke kant het bevestigingspunt op wijst. X-as (de draaiing): zodra Z vastligt kan de beugel nog om Z draaien. X legt die klokstand vast. Y-as (automatisch): zodra Z en X bekend zijn volgt de derde loodrechte as automatisch. origin = waar zit het punt? Z = welke kant kijkt het punt op? X = hoe is het rond die richting gedraaid? Y = volgt automatisch
data.parent-a-topology-backed#Parent A: topol: The frame side can use a real face/edge/corner. For an edge/corner origin SolidCraft derives its frame from the selected geometry and keeps the topology by name, so it can follow dimension changes.
data.the-real-solidcraft-relationship-remains:
Forge still lowers the frame to SolidCraft’s own joint information. The readable names do not change the native data model.
A — frame side edge + on + corner can select real topology. SolidCraft keeps that selection associated with changing geometry. B — bracket side point + z + x explicitly supplies the child joint origin and its orientation.
data.the-rear-row-is-the-same-idea-from-the-o: Corner Parent anchor Child point Parent z Parent x Current child input Top left Anchor.BACK_TOP_LEFT A +Y +X z=-Y, x=+X Top right Anchor.BACK_TOP_RIGHT B +Y -Z z=-Y, x=+X Bottom right Anchor.BACK_BOTTOM_RIGHT A +Y -X z=-Y, x=+X Bottom left Anchor.BACK_BOTTOM_LEFT B +Y +Z z=-Y, x=+X These values describe the current HUB75 assembly implementation; they are evidence for understanding the native joint frames, not a proposal for the final Forge API.
data.the-same-idea-in-forge#The same idea in:
For the six main axis directions, Forge uses readable names instead of requiring the vector every time:
Forge Vector Direction Anchor.RIGHT (1, 0, 0) +X Anchor.LEFT (-1, 0, 0) -X Anchor.BACK (0, 1, 0) +Y Anchor.FRONT (0, -1, 0) -Y Anchor.UP (0, 0, 1) +Z Anchor.DOWN (0, 0, -1) -Z AnchorFrame( origin=(10, 25, 0), z=Anchor.RIGHT, x=Anchor.UP, ) These names are only readable unit vectors. They do not add a second orientation system. Arbitrary XYZ vectors remain valid for genuinely angled frames.
data.the-two-points-used-by-the-current-hub75:
The reusable CornerBracket does not store these as named anchors. The assembly currently chooses two points on the neutral bracket geometry:
I = (0, 0, 0) # inside corner / component origin A = (0, 0, -w) # one arm thickness below I B = (w, 0, 0) # one arm thickness right of I For the front row, both A and B use the same current child-frame directions:
joint z = +Y = (0, 1, 0) # out through the broad bracket face joint x = -Z = (0, 0, -1) # down along the bracket profile For the rear row, the current assembly uses:
joint z = -Y = (0, -1, 0) # opposite broad bracket face joint x = +X = (1, 0, 0) # right along the bracket profile
